summary.text: Define \(L_0=4,L_1=16,L_2=63\) and \(L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\), and set \(D_n=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n\). The recurrence \(D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\), together with the growth bounds \(0<D_n\le 4\cdot3^n\le L_n\), gives \(L_{n+2}<L_{n+1}^2/L_n\le L_{n+2}+1\); thus the ceiling-minus-one rule always returns \(L_{n+2}\), proving the claimed linear recurrence and hence the generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, once \(b_n,b_{n+1}>0\), the next term is the greatest integer \(m\) for which
\[
\frac{m}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
Because the two denominators are positive, this inequality is equivalent to
\[
m<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}.
\]
For any positive real number \(r\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(r\) is \(\lceil r\rceil-1\), whether or not \(r\) is itself an integer. Consequently the original recursion can be written as
\[
b_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
For positive integers \(x,y\), one also has
\[
\left\lceil\frac{x}{y}\right\rceil
 =\left\lfloor\frac{x+y-1}{y}\right\rfloor,
\]
so (1) is precisely the integer recursion
\[
b_{n+2}=\left\lfloor\frac{b_{n+1}^2+b_n-1}{b_n}\right\rfloor-1. \tag{2}
\]
We shall prove that this nonlinear recursion in fact agrees with a linear one.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((L_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
L_0=4,\qquad L_1=16,\qquad L_2=63,
\]
and
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{3}
\]
The main task is to prove that every \(L_n\) is positive and that
\[
L_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{4}
\]
Once this is known, the initial conditions and induction will imply \(b_n=L_n\) for every \(n\).

We begin with a growth estimate for \(L_n\):
\[
L_n>0\quad\text{and}\quad 3L_n\le L_{n+1}\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{5}
\]
For \(n=0\), this says \(4>0\) and \(12\le16\). For \(n=1\), it says \(16>0\) and \(48\le63\). We now use strong induction. Suppose the assertions at all earlier indices are available, and consider an index of the form \(n+2\). Positivity of \(L_{n+2}\) follows at once from the earlier growth inequalities (indeed, \(L_{n+2}\ge3L_{n+1}>0\)). Moreover, by (3),
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n.
\]
The earlier growth inequalities imply \(L_{n+2}\ge L_n\) (in fact they imply the stronger \(L_{n+2}\ge9L_n\)). Therefore
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n\ge 3L_{n+2}.
\]
This proves (5) at the next index and completes the induction.

We next measure the discrepancy between the square \(L_{n+1}^2\) and the neighboring product \(L_nL_{n+2}\). Define
\[
D_n=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n. \tag{6}
\]
A direct use of the recurrence (3) gives the important identity
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n. \tag{7}
\]
For completeness, put
\[
a=L_n,\quad b=L_{n+1},\quad c=L_{n+2},\quad d=L_{n+3}=4c-a.
\]
Then \(L_{n+4}=4d-b\) and \(L_{n+5}=4(4d-b)-c\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{n+3}
 &=L_{n+4}^2-L_{n+5}L_{n+3}\\
 &=(4d-b)^2-(16d-4b-c)d\\
 &=b^2-4bd+cd.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
4D_{n+1}+D_n
 &=4(c^2-db)+(b^2-ca)\\
 &=b^2-4bd+c(4c-a)\\
 &=b^2-4bd+cd,
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves (7).

The first few terms needed for the initial discrepancy calculation are
\[
L_0=4,\quad L_1=16,\quad L_2=63,
\]
\[
L_3=4\cdot63-4=248,
\qquad
L_4=4\cdot248-16=976.
\]
Thus
\[
D_0=16^2-63\cdot4=4,
\]
\[
D_1=63^2-248\cdot16=1,
\]
and
\[
D_2=248^2-976\cdot63=16.
\]
We claim the following simultaneous positivity and upper bound:
\[
0<D_n\le 4\cdot3^n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{8}
\]
The displayed values verify this for \(n=0,1,2\): they are respectively \(4,1,16\), while the corresponding upper bounds are \(4,12,36\).

For the induction step, assume the bound for \(D_n\) and \(D_{n+1}\). By (7),
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n>0.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{n+3}
 &\le 4(4\cdot3^{n+1})+4\cdot3^n\\
 &=52\cdot3^n\\
 &\le108\cdot3^n
 =4\cdot3^{n+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Strong induction, beginning with the three initial cases, proves (8).

The growth estimate (5) also yields a lower bound for \(L_n\):
\[
4\cdot3^n\le L_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, equality holds at \(n=0\), and if \(4\cdot3^n\le L_n\), then
\[
4\cdot3^{n+1}=3(4\cdot3^n)\le3L_n\le L_{n+1}.
\]
Combining (8) and (9), we obtain
\[
0<D_n\le L_n. \tag{10}
\]

We now show that (10) is exactly what is needed for the ceiling recursion. From the definition (6), the strict inequality \(D_n>0\) says
\[
L_{n+2}L_n<L_{n+1}^2. \tag{11}
\]
The upper bound \(D_n\le L_n\) says
\[
L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n\le L_n,
\]
or equivalently
\[
L_{n+1}^2\le(L_{n+2}+1)L_n. \tag{12}
\]
Since \(L_n>0\), dividing (11) and (12) by \(L_n\) gives
\[
L_{n+2}<\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\le L_{n+2}+1. \tag{13}
\]
The unique conclusion from (13) is
\[
\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil=L_{n+2}+1,
\]
and therefore
\[
\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1=L_{n+2},
\]
which is (4).

One can also see explicitly that this matches the integer-division form (2). Set
\[
x=L_{n+1}^2,\qquad y=L_n,\qquad q=L_{n+2}.
\]
From \(qy<x\), and the fact that all quantities are integers, we get \(qy\le x-1\), hence
\[
(q+1)y\le x+y-1.
\]
From \(x\le(q+1)y\), together with \(y>0\), we get
\[
x+y-1<(q+2)y.
\]
Thus
\[
q+1\le\frac{x+y-1}{y}<q+2,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{x+y-1}{y}\right\rfloor=q+1.
\]
Subtracting one gives \(q=L_{n+2}\), exactly as required by (2).

Although the \(L_n\) were initially defined as integers, (5) shows that they are positive integers. We may therefore regard them as natural numbers without changing their values. In particular, equation (3) is also a valid natural-number recurrence: its right-hand side is nonnegative because it equals the positive integer \(L_{n+3}\). Thus natural-number subtraction causes no truncation, and
\[
L_{n+3}=4L_{n+2}-L_n
\]
has its usual integer meaning.

We can now identify the original sequence with \(L\). We prove by strong induction that
\[
b_n=L_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{14}
\]
At \(n=0\) and \(n=1\), this follows from the common initial values \(4\) and \(16\). At \(n=2\), either (4) or a direct calculation gives
\[
b_2=\left\lceil\frac{16^2}{4}\right\rceil-1=64-1=63=L_2.
\]
Now suppose the equality is known through indices \(n\) and \(n+1\). Applying the original recursion (1), the induction hypothesis, and (4), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+2}
 &=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=L_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This completes the induction and proves (14). In particular, positivity of the auxiliary sequence also proves retrospectively that every denominator appearing in the original extremal-ratio construction is positive.

It follows immediately from (3) and (14) that the original sequence satisfies
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
b_{n+3}=4b_{n+2}-b_n. \tag{15}
\]
Equivalently, for every \(m\ge3\),
\[
b_m=4b_{m-1}-b_{m-3}. \tag{16}
\]
This is the conjectured linear recurrence.

Finally, let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, regarded first as a formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^0\) in \((1-4x+x^3)G(x)\) is \(b_0=4\). The coefficient of \(x^1\) is
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0.
\]
The coefficient of \(x^2\) is
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
For each \(n\ge3\), the coefficient is
\[
b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3},
\]
which is zero by (16). Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)=4-x^2.
\]
Since the polynomial \(1-4x+x^3\) has constant term \(1\), it is invertible as a formal power series, and hence
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Thus the sequence produced by the original greatest-integer consecutive-ratio rule has exactly the conjectured generating function.
